47-073.r: Pabna rebellion → 1873-85 (intense 1873-1876; Bengal Tenancy Act 1885 met its demand); Eka Movement → 1922; Santhal Rebellion → 1855-56; Tana Bhagat Movement → 1914.

47-074.r: Eka movement (1921-22) → farmers of Hardoi, Bahraich, Sitapur etc. in U.P., against rent 50% above the agreed amount; led by Madari Pasi.

47-075.r: Rampa Rebellion → 1879-80; Pabna Peasant Revolt → 1873-76; Bengal Indigo Revolt → 1859-60; Jaintia Rebellion → 1860-63.

47-076.r: Moplah revolt of 1921 → Malabar, Kerala; mostly Muslim tenants against Hindu landlords' exploitation.

47-077.r: 'Moplah Revolt' (1921) → Malabar region of Kerala; Muslim tenants rose over no security of tenure, renewal fees and high rent.

47-078.r: Barrackpur Mutiny → November 1824; Berhampur Revolt → February 1857; Santhal Revolt → 1855-56; Vellore Mutiny → July 1806.

47-080.r: Wrong pair: Chuar revolt - Madhya Pradesh. Correct: Moplah revolt - Kerala (1921, linked to Khilafat); Kuka revolt - Punjab; Koli revolt - Gujarat (Taranga hills, Mehsana).

47-081.r: Bhil revolt (1818-1831) → Khandesh, in today's Maharashtra and M.P.; British took Khandesh in 1818; Trimbakji, Baji Rao II's minister, instigated it.

47-082.r: Wrong pair: Nayak - Tana Bhagat → Tana Bhagat (1914) was of Chota Nagpur Oraons, begun by Jatra Oraon. Correct: Munda - Birsa; Santhal - Kanhu; Ahom - Gomdhar Kunwar.

47-084.r: Kuki revolt → Tripura (and Manipur), 1917-19; Kuka revolt → Punjab; Pabna revolt → Bengal (1873-1876); Birsa Munda revolt → Bihar (now Jharkhand).
47-084.t: Don't confuse Kuki (Tripura, Manipur) with Kuka (Punjab).

47-085.r: Kuka rebellion began in the 1840s (Bhagat Jawahar Mal), not 1832-34; Kuki rebellion began in 1917 (against Labour Corps for WWI), not 1860-90.
47-085.c: Both (c) Kuki 1860-90 and (d) Kuka 1832-34 are wrong pairs, so the book says the question should be cancelled or both answers accepted.

47-086.r: Paika Rebellion (1817, Khordha) → Bakshi Jagabandhu Bidyadhar Mahapatra; Bareilly Rebellion (1816) → Mufti Muhammad Aiwaz; Malabar → Edachana Kungan; Sylhet → Radharam.

47-087.r: Bhumij revolt (1832-33, Jungle Mahal; began over Barabhum zamindari succession) → led by Ganga Narain.

47-088.r: Tebhaga Movement (1946-47, Bengal) → led by Bangiya Pradeshik Kisan Sabha; sharecroppers demanded landlord's share cut to 1/3 (Floud Commission); leaders Kampram Singh, Bhuvan Singh.

47-089.r: First tribal leader inspired by Gandhi → Haipou Jadonang, Naga leader of Manipur, who worked with Rani Gaidinliu.

47-090.r: First organiser of labour movement in India → N.M. Lokhande (1848-1897), for cotton mill workers.

48-001.r: First Madarsa set up by the British → Calcutta, 1780, by Warren Hastings.

48-002.r: Asiatic Society of Bengal → Sir William Jones (judge at Calcutta), with Warren Hastings' backing; first Sanskrit college at Varanasi → Jonathan Duncan.

48-004.r: Asiatic Society (1784) founded under Warren Hastings (GG 1774-85), an orientalist backing Sanskrit, Persian, Arabic; he declined its Presidentship for William Jones. A and R true, R explains A.

48-005.r: Raja Rammohan Roy → offered membership of the Societe Asiatique of Paris (founded 1822); he founded the Brahmo Sabha in 1828.

48-006.r: First English translation of the Bhagavad Gita → Charles Wilkins; preface by Warren Hastings.

48-007.r: First English translation of Kalidasa's 'Abhigyan Shakuntalam' → Sir William Jones.

48-008.r: Main reason the British spread modern education → need for educated Indians in minor administrative posts, which also cut administrative cost.

48-009.r: First grant for education (Rs one lakh, i.e. 100,000 a year) → Charter Act 1813; it also ended Company's trade monopoly except tea and China trade.

48-010.r: Wood's Despatch (1854) → grants-in-aid system and universities at Calcutta, Madras, Bombay on London University model; not English at all levels. 1 and 2 correct.

48-011.r: Wood's Despatch (19 July 1854, by Charles Wood, President of Board of Control) → English medium for higher studies; stress on female education and vocational training. Both correct.

48-012.r: Wood's Despatch → education; issued 19 July 1854; called the 'Magna Carta' of English education in India; education department in every province.

48-014.r: Hunter Commission (1882, W.W. Hunter, set up by Lord Ripon) → first Indian Education Commission; special stress on primary education.

48-016.r: National Council of Education, Bengal → 15 August 1906; grew out of the Rangpur National School (1905).

48-017.r: Sadler Commission (1917) → education: studied Calcutta University; chairman M.E. Sadler (Leeds VC); Indian members Ashutosh Mukherjee and Zia-ud-din Ahmad.

48-019.r: Curzon's University Commission (1902, chair Thomas Raleigh) → Indian members Syed Hussain Bilgrami and Justice Gurudas Banerjee; led to the Universities Act 1904.

48-020.r: Sargent Plan of education → 1944; free, compulsory basic education for children 6-14; more vocational and scientific outlook.

48-021.r: Lord Macaulay → English education; Bentinck accepted his report; Resolution of 1835 made English the language of education and official use.

48-022.r: 'Downward Filtration Theory' → education: educate the upper classes, who would pass knowledge down to the masses; propounded by Macaulay.

48-024.r: Foundation of modern education → Macaulay's Minute, 2 February 1835: "a single shelf of a good European library was worth the whole literature of India and Arabia".
48-024.t: Not Wood's Despatch (1854) or Hunter Commission (1882) - those came later.

48-026.r: "The Company is an anomaly but it is part of a system where everything is an anomaly" → T.B. Macaulay, Law Member (1834-1838) who drafted the Indian Penal Code.

48-027.r: English education in India came via all three: Charter Act 1813, General Committee of Public Instruction (1823), Orientalist-Anglicist controversy; introduced under Bentinck.

48-029.r: First three universities (Calcutta, Madras, Bombay) → 1857, on the London University model, as proposed by Wood's Despatch 1854.

48-030.r: First Women's University (Bombay) → D.K. Karve, who also opened a home for widows in Poona (1896) and backed widow remarriage.

48-031.r: Deccan Education Society (1884) → B.G. Tilak, Agarkar, Chiplunkar, Namjoshi; Justice Ranade was only a patron, not a founder.

48-032.r: Muhammadan Anglo-Oriental College, Aligarh → founded 1875 (as Madarsatul Uloom) by Sir Syed Ahmad Khan; renamed MAO College 1877; Aligarh Muslim University 1920.

48-033.r: Principal of M.A.O. College, Aligarh, who encouraged Muslim separatism in the late 19th century → Theodore Beck.

48-034.r: Earliest: Hindu College, Calcutta (1817, Rammohan Roy with David Hare) → Delhi College (1824) → Mayo College, Ajmer (1875).

48-037.r: Initial aim of the Aligarh Movement (Sir Syed Ahmad Khan) → spread Western scientific education among Indian Muslims.

48-038.r: Only 2 correct: Calcutta Madarsa → Warren Hastings (1780). Sanskrit College Banaras → Jonathan Duncan (1791), not William Jones; Fort William College → Richard Wellesley (1800), not Arthur.
48-038.t: Fort William College was Richard Wellesley's, not Arthur Wellesley's.

48-039.r: Fort William College (10 July 1800, Wellesley) → to train British civilians for administration in India.
